6.4.5 Switching Data Between the Staging Manager and Original
Tables
You can use the staging function data switching to quickly exchange data between the staging
area and original tables. This allows you to implement various strategies to reduce the down-
time. Data switching can also be used for client staging. However, the switch is much quicker
when using shadow tables.
6.4.5.1 Staging with Shadow Tables
When conducting a data switch for transparent original tables and shadow tables using the
DDIC Manager, the tables will be renamed so that they switch positions. Data stored in the
shadow table will be stored in the original table and vice versa. You can conduct the data switch
again to undo this process.
6.4.5.2 Staging with Differing Target Clients
The Staging Manager type C uses differing target clients as staging areas. The switch is con-
ducted by updating the client field in the table. This makes it possible to switch cluster and pool
tables without conversion into transparent tables. You can conduct the data switch again to
undo this process.
Proceed as follows to conduct a data switch:
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter548

=====PAGE 549=====
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/SG.
The program SNP SG - Direct control for Staging opens.
2. Enter the tables you want to switch.
3. Select the Staging Manager type.
4. Optional: Define a target area ID.

6.5 Comparing Staging Data with Original Tables
For various reasons, it may be necessary to compare data between different staging areas or to
compare data between staging and original tables.
Use transaction /N/SNP/SG_COMPARE to compare the data. The following values are cal-
culated per table:
The difference in numbers of rows between the comparison areas
The number of differences in key fields – the number of records missing in the comparison
areas per table
The number of differences in rows – the number of records with differing non-key fields in
the comparison areas per table
To compare data in staging area tables and original tables, you must enter the following para-
meters:
Tables: Names of the tables for comparison
Transparent tables only: Ensures that cluster and pool tables are not included in the com-
parison (due to the performance impact)
Left/right staging manager: Specifies the type of staging used in the comparison (DDIC
or client)
Left/right target area: Identifies the staging area used in the comparison
Original tables: Causes that original tables are used as the target comparison area
Another target area: Enables the use of a second target area for the comparison (com-
parison between two target areas will take place)
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter549

=====PAGE 550=====
The performance of a comparison on cluster tables is much slower than on transparent tables.
Proceed as follows to compare two versions of a rule:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/SG_COMPARE.
2. Enter the tables whose data you want to compare.
3. In the Left staging manager field, specify a type.
4. In the Left target area field, specify a target area.
5. Click
Execute.
The comparison has been performed.
Proceed as follows to perform a comparison with cluster tables/pool tables:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/SG_COMPARE.
2. Enter the tables whose data you want to compare.
3. Disable the Transparent tables only option.
4. In the Left staging manager field, specify a type.
5. In the Left target area field, specify a target area.
6. Click
Execute.
The comparison has been performed.
6.6 Rollback of Logged Write Modes
The staging framework allows you to log write accesses to tables. The write modes INSLOG,
DELLOG, MODLOG and LOGADK are used. The relevant write modes change the target tables
block by block via the SQL statements INSERT, DELETE, MODIFY or INSERT ACCEPTING
DUPLICATE KEY and store both the new and the old data in staging. The relevant shadow
tables or staging clients also depend on the target area ID. However, they are different from
those used for writing to staging and the data switch.
The log can be used to undo the changes made to the respective tables. This undoes all
changes to the respective tables that were made by specifying the relevant target area and
using the mentioned write modes.
NOTE
The extent to which the rollback leaves a consistent system depends on the cir-
cumstances in which it is used and the selection of tables. For example, undoing
changes in running production systems is only recommended with precise control,
since written data could already have been further processed.
Proceed as follows to roll back changes:
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter550

=====PAGE 551=====
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/SG_ROLLBACK.
The program Rollback of changes based on staging log opens.
2. Enter the tables for which you want to roll back changes.
3. Specify the staging manager type you want to use.
4. Select the write mode you used to perform the changes.
5. Enter the number of processes you want to use.
6. Click
Execute.
The Monitor for staging rollback opens.
The rollback is performed in the background.
You can monitor the operation in the monitor for staging rollback.

7 Test Data Synthesizer
Test Data Synthesizer (TDS) is a tool that generates synthetic, or artificial, test data. This allows
you to perform representative tests with mass data, even in development systems and project
systems, which do not usually contain much data. You can also perform destructive tests with
synthetic data, even in production systems. This is useful for testing the runtime and scalability
of new software functions as well as for testing the system configuration and sizing.
For this purpose, test tables are created in the Z namespace with a user-specific prefix. You can
either copy these tables along with the data or generate data into these tables. You can also
copy tables with generated data to reduce the runtime of the data preparation for repeated tests
that are destructive to the data used.
The following chapters provide information and instructions on how to use Test Data Syn-
thesizer.
7.1 Roles and Authorizations
The currently valid role overview is available in the chapter Roles and Authorizations for the
SNP Software Components AN, TF and MC.
NOTE
To perform a migration in the SNP S/4HANA Cockpit, you require the authorization
object FINS_MIG with the activity 16.
NOTE
In order to generate and activate CDS views in the SNP S/4HANA Cockpit, you
require the authorization object S_DEVELOP.

User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter558

=====PAGE 559=====
If the options Generate with domain values and/or Generate with value tables are disabled, or
if table fields are included for which no values from domains or value tables exist, the data is cre-
ated using an algorithm. This algorithm is based on natural numbers and starts with 1 for empty
tables. The algorithm can also continue the generation in already filled tables or in tables with
already existing data. In such cases, the highest number is automatically determined from the
already existing data and the generation algorithm is continued. If you enter a value in the field
Record counts to skip, this value is the minimum starting number. Tables with only “syn-
thetically” generated key fields have the same key in different clients if they were generated with
the same natural number. This option allows you to control the number of duplicate records in
multiple clients for tests in which this is important.
NOTE
You can also use this function via the Fiori Launchpad.

8.1 Introduction
The Posting Engine is a migration component that operates independently of tables, enabling
the seamless transfer of documents from the source SAP system to the designated target SAP
system. It is integrated with the Transformation Cockpit and in table-based migrations. It also
uses the TC mapping and the domain rules. This enables hybrid or purely posting-based migra-
tion approaches. A separate web interface is available for evaluating the posting results.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter564

=====PAGE 565=====
8.1.1 Areas of Application of the Posting Engine
8.1.1.1 Open item and balance approach
In this approach, only aggregated balances and open items are migrated (along with cus-
tomizing and master data). In such a scenario, the Posting Engine simplifies the selections and
transformation rules. It also adds an additional layer of security, therefore reducing the effort
required for business tests.
You can add a further measure for automatic data quality assurance by applying Data Con-
sistency Verification on the data that is staged in the Posting Engine.
8.1.1.2 Complex selection for a carve-out
If customizing and business processes differ greatly between the source and target systems, for
example in profit center carve-outs, carve-outs driven by logistics or migrations into a com-
pletely new greenfield template, table-based migration rules can become very complex. Here,
the Posting Engine can help to simplify the data migration and therefore reduce the workload
unless the data history is required.
8.1.1.3 Merge into existing company codes
When merging data into existing company codes, the use of postings can simplify rules and
reduce risk.
8.1.1.4 Migrations during the uptime
Postings do not require a downtime if they are used exclusively.
8.1.1.5 No S/4 conversion is necessary
Posted data does not need to be converted.
8.1.1.6 Non-SAP legacy systems (including custom solutions)
Postings are recommended when integrating data from any source other than legacy SAP Busi-
ness Suite systems.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter565

=====PAGE 566=====

8.3.4 Transformation
In the Transformation tab, you can move data objects to the corresponding blocks in the Trans-
formation folder using drag & drop.
Within the export block, a range of data sources is available, facilitating the export of business
objects to the target system. The staging tables /SNP/TE_FI_OPSEL and /SNP/TE_FI_PK are
populated based on the provided filters. You can perform the execution by right-clicking the rel-
evant block and choosing to execute it either in the background or in dialog. After a successful
export, a green icon (
) appears next to the block.
The import block is used to generate staging tables for the Posting Engine if they do not already
exist. These tables are then populated with the previously exported data. This approach ensures
a dynamic, simple and generic process for any BAPI.
In the final step, you can execute the posting object to post the provided data via the Post API.
This eliminates the need to manually specify BAPI signatures and static code for the data pre-
paration. The results of the posting operation are recorded in the log tables.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter569

=====PAGE 570=====
If you have performed these three steps and a green icon (
) appears in the Status column for
each step, all the data has been successfully posted to the target system.

8.6 Using Postings in Projects
8.6.1 Introduction
This guide will provide you a comprehensive understanding of the posting-based data migration
approach when transitioning to SAP® S/4HANA. The Posting Engine is a core component of
SNP’s software portfolio for data migrations, offering a seamless and secure method for trans-
ferring financial documents from a source system to an SAP® S/4HANA target system.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter577

=====PAGE 578=====
8.6.2 Overview of Posting-Based Data Migration
The journey to SAP® S/4HANA is a significant step for any organization looking to modernize its
ERP landscape and embrace digital transformation. One of the critical aspects of this transition
is the migration of financial data, which must be executed with precision to ensure business con-
tinuity and compliance. The Posting Engine facilitates this process by enabling the migration of
financial documents through postings, which are integrated with the Transformation Cockpit and
table-based migrations. This integration allows for a hybrid or purely posting-based migration
approach, leveraging the mapping and domain rules of the Transformation Cockpit to ensure
data integrity and consistency.
8.6.3 Use Cases for the Posting Engine
The Posting Engine is particularly advantageous in scenarios where:
Only aggregated balances and open items are migrated along with customizing and mas-
ter data, known as the open item and balance approach.
Complex selections are required for carve-outs or when the customizing and business pro-
cesses significantly differ between the source and target systems.
Data is merged into existing company codes, where the use of postings can facilitate the
migration rules and reduce the risk of errors.
Migrations need to continue during the uptime, because postings do not require a system
downtime if used exclusively.
8.6.4 Key Advantages of the Posting Engine
No need for S/4 conversion of posted data.
Supports non-SAP legacy systems and custom solutions, making it ideal for data integ-
ration from various sources.
Reduces the complexity and workload of the data migration, especially in scenarios where
the data history is not required.
Adds an additional security layer and reduces the testing effort for business users through
automated data quality assurance.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter578

=====PAGE 579=====
8.6.5 General Workflow of the Posting Engine
The Posting Engine workflow consists of several phases:
Implementation: Creating selections, uploading mappings, defining migration rules, and
setting posting parameters.
Staging: Selecting open items and balances from index and balance tables in the source
system, adding data to the global staging area, and making it available across generated
staging tables for a specific function.
Rule application: Moving data to the target, applying mappings and rules, and preparing
the data for posting.
Posting: Starting the simulation or posting, analyzing posting errors, and maintaining
potential solutions. This documentation will guide you through each of these phases,
providing detailed instructions and best practices to ensure a successful data migration to
SAP S/4HANA using the Posting Engine. We look forward to embarking on this journey
together, ensuring that your financial data is migrated efficiently, accurately and securely
to your new SAP S/4HANA environment.
8.6.6 Posting-Based vs. Table-Based Data Migration Approaches
When considering the transition to SAP® S/4HANA, organizations must choose between vari-
ous data migration strategies. There are two main approaches: posting-based migration and
table-based migration. Each has its advantages and challenges, and the choice largely depends
on the specific needs and circumstances of the business.
8.6.7 Table-Based Data Migration Approach
Advantages:
Historical data migration: Table-based migrations can selectively or fully migrate his-
torical data, maintaining reporting continuity and compliance.
Efficiency with large data volumes: High levels of parallelization in the data migration
allow for much shorter downtimes when migrating large amounts of data.
Near-zero downtime: This approach enables the source system to keep operating with
minimal business impact during the migration.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter579

=====PAGE 580=====
Flexible go-live date: Table-based migrations can be performed independently of period
or fiscal year closings, offering more flexibility and reducing risks.
Completeness of data: Customer data models and standard data models that are not fully
covered by interfaces can be migrated at the table level.
Consistent document linkage: Maintaining the integrity and continuity of transaction his-
tories and related documents is crucial for financial reporting and audits.
Disadvantages:
Complexity in transformations: Table-based migrations can become complex when
extensive transformations and data creations are required to fit new business structures.
System consolidation challenges: Although a system consolidation can reduce IT com-
plexity, it can also be a complex process that requires careful planning and execution.
Potential for data inconsistencies: Direct table access requires more intensive testing
and validation to ensure data quality and consistency.
Longer project timelines: Large-scale table-based migrations require extensive planning
and long execution times, which can extend the overall project duration.
In summary, the decision between posting-based and table-based data migration approaches
should be based on a detailed analysis of the organization’s requirements, data volume, system
complexity, and the desired future state of the SAP® S/4HANA environment. Each approach
has its benefits and must be aligned with the strategic goals of the migration project.
8.6.8 Closing Migrated Items/Documents in the Source System
When performing a posting-based migration to close migrated items/documents in the source
system, you must follow a structured approach to ensure data integrity and compliance. Follow
these steps to close migrated items/documents in the source system:
Data validation: Before starting the posting process, perform a comprehensive data val-
idation to ensure that the items/documents you want to close are accurate and complete.
Posting preparation: Prepare the data for posting by ensuring that all necessary map-
pings, rules and parameters are configured correctly within the Posting Engine.
Simulation: Start a simulation of the posting process to identify any potential errors or
inconsistencies that can arise during the actual posting.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter580

=====PAGE 581=====
Posting execution: Once the simulation is successfully completed, proceed with the
actual posting of the migrated items/documents, ensuring that the process is closely mon-
itored for any errors or exceptions.
Error handling: Correct any posting errors promptly to maintain data accuracy and com-
pleteness.
By following these steps, you can effectively close migrated items/documents in the source sys-
tem, facilitating a seamless and controlled transition to the target SAP® S/4HANA environment.
8.6.9 Managing Posting Runtimes Effectively
Generally, SNP employs a strategic project blueprint which includes multiple test migrations to
ensure a seamless and efficient transfer. By doing so, posting runtimes can be managed during
migrations into running production systems. The process is structured as follows:
Initial analysis and planning: Before any migration activities begin, a detailed analysis of
the current system and data volume is performed. This helps customers to understand the
scope and complexity of the migration project. The project blueprint is then drafted, out-
lining the steps and strategies to be implemented.
Test migrations: SNP usually plans for three or four test migrations. These test migrations
are important to measure actual posting runtimes and to identify potential bottlenecks or
issues that impact the migration process. During these tests, different data posting
strategies are evaluated to determine the most efficient approach.
Runtime measurement and estimation: During the first test migrations, the posting
runtimes are carefully measured. This data is used to estimate the expected runtimes for
the actual migration. If the posting runtimes are too long, adjustments to the migration
strategy or system sizing are necessary.
Migration strategy development: Based on the insights gained from the test migrations, a
migration strategy is developed. This strategy might include starting postings during the
uptime of the target system to distribute the load and minimize the impact on the system
performance. For large data volumes, a hybrid approach which combines table-based and
posting-based migrations can be employed.
System sizing: Appropriate system sizing is crucial to handle the data volume efficiently.
The hardware and system resources must be scaled to meet the requirements of the
migration process without causing excessive downtime or system strain.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter581

=====PAGE 582=====
Uptime posting: One part of the strategy includes initiating postings during the uptime of
the target system to manage posting runtimes effectively. This allows for a more con-
tinuous migration process and helps to reduce the overall downtime required for the migra-
tion.
Hybrid migration approach: In a hybrid SAP-to-SAP migration project, the main migration
can be table-based to transfer large volumes of data quickly. Postings then continue dur-
ing or after this phase, leveraging the system’s uptime to complete the process. This
approach helps to balance the load and ensures that the system remains operational for
users.
Continuous monitoring and optimization: It is necessary to constantly monitor the migra-
tion process to ensure that the posting runtimes remain within the expected thresholds. If
any deviations are observed, immediate action can be taken to optimize the process and
adjust the strategy as required.
By following this structured approach and leveraging SNP’s expertise in data migrations, com-
panies can manage posting runtimes effectively and ensure a successful migration to the target
system with minimal disruption to ongoing business operations.
8.6.10 Handling Dependencies Between Documents
During a posting-based data migration, the handling of dependencies between business objects
and documents is an important task to ensure the integrity and continuity of transaction data. In
SAP, documents are often linked together to display the transaction flow and to maintain a clear
audit trail. For example, in the sales document flow, there is a typical sequence that starts with a
sales order, followed by delivery, and finally the billing document. Each of these documents is
dependent on the preceding one. This linkage must be preserved during the migration.
However, not all linkages can be preserved during a posting-based migration. For example, in
the Financial Accounting (FI) module, FI documents are linked to source documents through
fields like AWTYP (Reference Transaction) and AWKEY (Reference Key) in the table BKPF
(Accounting Document Header). These linkages are crucial for tracing to the original trans-
action. In a posting-based migration, recreating these linkages can be challenging because the
migration needs to follow a specific sequence, in which dependent objects can only be posted
after the objects they depend on have been posted.
The sequential dependency has a significant negative impact on the testability of dependent
migration objects. Testing becomes more complex because it is not possible to post or to
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter582

=====PAGE 583=====
simulate dependent business objects without first posting the objects they rely on. For example,
you cannot post an invoice without first posting the corresponding delivery and sales order. Due
to this limitation, there are delays in the migration process and difficulties in validating data until
all dependent objects are successfully migrated.
To address these challenges, SNP utilizes table-based corrections after posting to recreate
some of the document linkages, especially in FI. This approach involves making direct adjust-
ments to the tables after the initial posting process to create the necessary linkages between the
documents. By following this approach, SNP ensures that the integrity of the document linkages
is maintained, even if the original posting sequence could not preserve these linkages.
In summary, posting-based data migrations have their limitations due to dependencies and the
need for a sequential posting process. However, SNP’s use of table-based corrections after the
migration helps to mitigate these issues by reestablishing critical document linkages, particularly
within the FI module. This ensures that the migrated data remains consistent and that the his-
torical audit trail is preserved.

9.1 Preparing Document Splits
This chapter illustrates the preparations required prior to performing the document split.
Proceed as follows to prepare the document split:
Set up the template scenario in Transformation Cockpit:
1. Download the template scenario.
2. In the menu bar, click Scenario > Upload scenario to insert the template.
3. Enter the SNP S/4HANA Cockpit target as the source and the target.
4. Add the BUKRS selection to your scenario.
5. Check and assign DSP_FLD_RESTORE.
6. Click
Save.
7. Start the run for the object DSP_TRANS_RESTORE_FIELDS.
NOTE
This step is only required if you need to restore fields with the report
/SNP/SP45_ACDOCA_BACKUP. If the option DSP_DIRECT_FIELD_
RESTORE is used, the mapping DSP_FLD_RESTORE is used directly by the
Transformation Cockpit object and the worklist report.
8. Set the parameter DSP_SEL_GJAHR_FROM.
9. Start the run /N/SNP/SP01_CHANGE_TAB_STRU in the control system.
10. Start transaction /N/SNP/SP45_BACKUP in the background.
11. Optional: Enable the Create package table option.
12. Adjust the package size.
13. Select the desired scenario.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter602

=====PAGE 603=====
14. Specify the company code.
15. Click
Execute.
The ACDOCA backup has been created.
9.2 Performing Document Splits
The document split function is required if you want to introduce a general ledger with document
split. The function applies specific split rules after the migration using Transformation Cockpit
and the SAP® S/4HANA Cockpit.
Prerequisites
The table ACDOCA has been generated using the SAP® S/4HANA Cockpit.
The document split customizing is available in the target system.
A backup has been created with the description Prepare document split.
Proceed as follows to perform a document split: 
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/TC.
2. Create a worklist by executing the Transformation Cockpit object DSP_SELECTION.
3. Check the selected ACDOCA entries against the customizing by executing the object
DSP_PRE_CHECK.
4. Check the results in the table /SNP/TE_DS_CHECK and report any errors to the company
or customer.
5. Create the table FAGL_SPLINFO (Transformation Cockpit object DSP_CREATE_FAGL_
SPLINFO).
NOTE
You can execute the object DSP_CREATE_FAGL_SPLINFO in parallel with
the backup.
6. Repost the table ACDOCA (Transformation Cockpit object DSP_REPOST_ACDOCA.
NOTE
The table ACDOCA is deleted. The split ACDOCA lines are inserted.
A backup is required for the execution.
The document split has been performed.
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter603

=====PAGE 604=====
NOTE
Iterative error handling: Check and correct the errors as described in the chapter
Report: Document Split Worklist. If necessary, adjust the configuration in the Global
parameters area and start a new iteration of the objects DSP_CREATE_FAGL_
SPLINFO and DSP_REPOST_ACDOCA until no more errors occur.
NOTE
Once the document split is complete, you can execute the object DSP_POST_
CHECK. This determines whether field information has been lost in the table
ACDOCA. The analysis is stored in the table /SNP/TE_DS_LOSTF.

9.4 Report: Document Split Worklist
The document split worklist report is used to display and process FI documents that are
included in the scope of the document split. Subsequently, you can create entries in the table
FAGL_SPLINFO and repost the table ACDOCA to build the GL view of the FI documents. This
view is built according to the document split rule defined in the SAP customizing. You can use
the report to analyze errors and apply methods for error handling. For mass processing, the cor-
responding TC object DSP_EXECUTE should be used.
Prerequisites:
An S/4HANA conversion has been performed in the target system (table ACDOCA has
been generated).
The document split customizing is available in the target system.
A backup of the table ACDOCA has been created (report /SNP/SP45_ACDOCA_
BACKUP).
A worklist has been created (export object DSP_SELECTION of the split scenario).
The first mass execution of the split has been performed (export object DSP_EXECUTE
of the split scenario).
User Guide - Kyano CrystalBridge Transformation Platzhalter607

=====PAGE 608=====
Proceed as follows to create the document split worklist report:

The Document split worklist window opens.
1. Specify the scenario for the document split.

the original table ACDOCA before the split are copied back to the split ACDOCA
rows. In the split scenario, you can define errors to be restored in the mapping
DSP_FLD_RESTORE.
Optional: Direct update (beta): If the table ACDOCA is updated, this will improve
the performance.

Downtime Optimization

=====PAGE 957=====
957
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
11 Downtime Optimization
11.1 About the Downtime Optimization
Downtime Optimization is based on the following three approaches. The following chapters
describe them in more detail:
Minimized Downtime on Target
RBNZD approach
NZD approach
11.2 Minimized Downtime on Target
NOTE
This subcomponent is still in the ramp-up phase. You may only use it after a separate
agreement (licensing).
Minimized Downtime on Target (MDT) is a software component and framework designed to allow
for selective migrations of organizational units to be performed in target systems with a significantly
shorter system downtime than other migration approaches. This is achieved by utilizing a separate
staging client that is created as a copy of the target client. Within the staging client, data can be
loaded via the Transformation Cockpit with all the necessary follow-on activities (i.e. S/4 con-
version, document split, verification and validation).
Once these activities are completed and the data is confirmed in its final format in the staging client,
a merge can be performed during the downtime from the staging client to the target production cli-
ent. In technical terms, this is achieved by updating the client fields for the tables in scope, effect-
ively moving the data from the staging client to the production client. If any collisions are identified
during the merge, i.e. primary key or secondary index values are identical between the clients, the
production client is always the leading client, and that data is maintained. An entry of the collision is
written to the paper bin client to maintain comprehensive documentation.
The technical runtime of MDT depends greatly on the specific project requirements, the size and
complexity of the migrated data, and the system environment. However, experience has shown that
the runtime of MDT is comparable to the pure technical import runtime of the Transformation Cock-
pit (without mappings and transformation rules, which typically make up most of the import
runtime). Therefore, the runtime of MDT is significantly shorter.

=====PAGE 958=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
958
The following conditions help to define when and how to use MDT and what requirements need to
be met.
While you can use MDT in a variety of use cases, it is especially valuable when implemented as
part of a wave-based approach. Furthermore, a wave-based migrations is possible by organ-
izational units, specifically by company codes.
As part of the MDT framework, three additional clients are created on a system at the beginning of
a project. They are the staging client itself where the data is loaded, a paper bin client where any
collisions detected between the staging and production clients are stored, and an import log client
that serves as a log of all loaded data.
Because the MDT framework requires the creation of at least three additional clients in a system
(staging, paper bin and import log), it is extremely important for a system to have enough disk
space to support the amount of data to be loaded – considering that the data will be loaded in dif-
ferent amounts to all previously mentioned clients. Depending on the size of the data volume that is
specified and loaded during the project, enough storage must be available to handle both the data
loaded into the staging client and the data saved to the import log client and the paper bin client. If
data replications (SAP SLT server), data intelligence or reporting take place, note that the MDT
activities might cause massive amounts of additional delta logs to be created.
In addition to disk space, a sufficient amount of memory must be available to support multiple pro-
cesses. The more processes MDT can use, the quicker the merge will happen. If the system runs
into memory issues during the migration or during the MDT activities, this can result in project
delays and data integrity issues.
The migration approach is as follows:
1. A staging client is created on the target production system using a client copy. It contains cus-
tomizing and master data for functional tests of the imported data. Furthermore, a paper bin
and import log client are created to maintain records of collisions and the complete data
records moved, respectively.
2.
Using the Transformation Cockpit, data is selected from the source system, exported, and
finally converted and imported into the staging client.
3. Functional tests, data consistency verifications and automated tests are performed in the sta-
ging client.

=====PAGE 959=====
959
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
4.
Minimized Downtime on Target deletes data from the staging client that was duplicated from
the target production client.
5. Minimized Downtime on Target moves data from the staging client to the production client,
therefore completing the migration. Duplicates that occurred after the deletion can be
handled in this step. Duplicates only have a negative effect on the runtime.
WARNING
The merge into the target production client is not reversible. No technical method exists
to guarantee that the migration is completely free of errors and inconsistencies. If errors
or inconsistencies occur, they must be corrected in the production client. Data that could
not be imported due to duplicates can be identified and revised because Minimized
Downtime on Target retains this data.
11.2.1 Roles and Authorizations
The currently valid role overview is available in the chapter Roles and Authorizations for the SNP
Software Components AN, TF and MC.
NOTE
To perform a migration in the SNP S/4HANA Cockpit, you require the authorization
object FINS_MIG with the activity 16.
NOTE
In order to generate and activate CDS views in the SNP S/4HANA Cockpit, you require
the authorization object S_DEVELOP.
11.2.2 Creating Staging Clients
As part of the MDT approach, a staging client is created from the production client. Minimized
Downtime on Target (MDT) transfers the staging data to the production system. This makes the
transformation process faster and more reliable.
This chapter is for experts who want to create staging clients and have the SAP knowledge
required to perform this operation.

=====PAGE 960=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
960
NOTE
The staging client numbers should not have been used before.
Proceed as follows to create a staging client from the production client:
1. Start transaction SCC4.
The view Display View “Clients”: Overview opens.
2. Click New Entries.
The view New Entries: Details of Added Entries opens.
3. Create the staging client with the desired values.
4. Click
Display/Change.
5. Log in to the staging client.
6. Start transaction SCC9.
The view Client Copy – Copy Client opens.
7. In the Selected profile field, select the value SAP_USER.
8. In the Source destination field, select the RFC connection of the production client.
9. Execute the copy process either as a background job or immediately.
10. Import the customizing and the master data including the selected tables.
You have created a staging client from a production client.
11.2.3 Counting Records and Collisions
This function allows you to count the data records in selected tables for specific clients – the staging
client and productive client. This enables you to record collisions between specific clients. If you
execute /N/SNP/MDT_CRAWL just before or during the Minimized Downtime on Target execution,
the progress and the estimated runtime will be calculated more accurately.
EXAMPLE
For example, a collision occurs for data records between two clients that have the same
values for primary keys and secondary indexes.
Proceed as follows to count data records:

=====PAGE 961=====
961
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT_CRAWL.
2. The window SNP Minimized Downtime on Target: Row counting opens.

11.2.4 Comparison of Changes in Staging with Production Data
This chapter explains how to perform a detailed collision comparison. This collision comparison
checks both primary keys and non-key fields. A collision occurs when the primary keys of a table
are the same on two clients, but the non-key fields are different.
As part of the MDT procedure, it is essential to verify whether the data loaded from production has
been modified in the staging client, potentially during validation tests or additional work. This step is
crucial because, during a data merge from the staging client to the production client, any duplicate
records with identical key field values will result in the data of the production client taking pre-
cedence and not being overwritten. Therefore, if changes were made in the staging client with the
aim of transferring them to production, this transfer will not occur. Instead, the conflicting data is
moved to the paper bin client, provided this setting is enabled, and the data in the production client
remains unchanged.
NOTE
You can use the detailed comparison and the evaluation reports for this check.
NOTE
Note that you cannot compare fields with certain data types (e.g. RSTR, LRAW, CTRL
and LCHR).

=====PAGE 963=====
963
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
Proceed as follows to perform a detailed collision comparison:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT_CMP_COL.
The view Compare collisions between clients opens.
2. Optional: Enter a program run description to clearly identify the run.
3. Specify the number of processes.
NOTE
Each process handles one table. Additional processes result in a shorter runtime. Any
number of processes higher than 50 must be confirmed by the user.
4. Optional: Select the Output results option.
NOTE
If selected, the results are output in table format at the end of the run. Otherwise, the out-
put is a workload ID and the table containing the results.
5. Specify the table scope that you want to compare.
6. Choose whether to include proxy objects in the analysis or not.
7. In the Client to check field, select the table that you want to check for changes.
8. In the Client to compare against field, select the client with the original data.
9. Select one of the following three options:
1. Count changed collisions: Counts the number of collisions for which any field of the
collision that is not the primary key differs in the check client compared to the compare
client.
2. Count distinct non-key val.: Counts the unique combinations of non-key column val-
ues and those not belonging to unique secondary indexes in both the check client and
the compare client for collision. If the count values are different, the data in the col-
lisions in the table has changed.
3. Primary key of changed coll.: Records the primary key values of collisions for which
any non-primary key field differs in the check client compared to the compare client.

=====PAGE 964=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
964
NOTE

which such a difference exists.
Max. table columns per check: Limits the number of non-key columns when com-
paring values between clients. If the table is too wide because it contains too
many columns, you can split a comparison into several comparisons in order to
speed up the process, depending on the parameter.
4. Count collisions and save keys: Executes the options 1 and 3 simultaneously.
10. Optional: Enable the option Save non-key field values.
NOTE

The values are saved as a string in both clients and separated using |(pipe sym-
bol). You can analyze them subsequently. See here for more information.
11. Optional: Enable the option Restrict number of saved collisions.
NOTE

This allows you to reduce memory consumption and the processing time.
12. Maintain the field Number of saved collisions.
NOTE

=====PAGE 972=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
972
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT.
2. Enter a program run description.
3. Optional: Adjust the Number of processes.
4. Optional: Enable the option Count rows for progress est.
5. If you enabled the option Count rows for progress est., specify the number of processes you
want to count.
6. Specify the tables for which you want to update the client field.
NOTE

7. Assign parameters to the tables in the section Limit selection of tables by table properties.

11. Optional: Disable the option Update proxy objects.

Overwrite staging from production: Data records with identical keys in the staging and
production clients are updated from the staging client to the paper bin client. After-
wards, all data records are copied from the production client to the staging client. If you
enable this option, you must specify the paper bin client and the load log client.
Replace collisions from production: Data records with identical keys in the staging
and production clients are updated from the staging client to the paper bin client. After-
wards, the data records are copied from the production client into the staging client. If
you enable this option, you must specify the paper bin client.
Delete collisions from staging: Data records with identical keys in the staging and pro-
duction clients are deleted from the staging client. 
Merge staging into production: The first execution is performed without a subselect. If
aborted, the execution is started with a subselect. If you enable this option, you can
decide whether you want to count the collisions.

=====PAGE 973=====
973
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
Move collisions to paper bin: Collisions (from the source) are moved to a paper bin cli-
ent, which overwrites duplicate data records in that client. If you enable this option, you
must specify the paper bin client.
No update: No data update is performed.
Copy collisions into paper bin: Data records with identical keys in the staging and pro-
duction clients are copied from the staging client into the paper bin client. This will over-
write duplicate records in the paper bin client. The staging and production clients
remain unchanged after executing the operation.
Copy staging into production: Data records with non-identical keys in the staging and
production clients are copied from the staging client into the production client. The sta-
ging client remains unchanged after executing the operation.
NOTE
Copying data from the staging client into production and subsequently mov-
ing it makes it impossible to document duplicate entries from an import in
staging. Move duplicates to the paper bin first.
Refresh data in staging 1:1: The records of the selected staging client will be
removed. Afterwards, all data records from the production client are added to the sta-
ging client. The production client remains unchanged during this process.

11.2.12 Retrieving Number Rules of the Next Number from Different
Clients
The design of Minimized Downtime on Target requires that the Transformation Cockpit first imports
data into a staging client. This intermediate step primarily serves as an additional safety measure
to enable functional tests. The final merge into the productive target client only takes place after
this step.
During imports into an existing client, new numbers from number ranges are often transferred to the
transformation rule base for all types of documents. Using Minimized Downtime on Target, these
numbers must be retrieved from the actual productive target client and reserved there. They must
not be reserved exclusively in the staging client.
NOTE
If the numbers were reserved exclusively in the staging client, duplicate numbers would
be generated due to the simultaneous operations in the production client. These cannot
be merged later due to duplicate keys.
To retrieve the numbers from the production client, the global function GF_NUMBER_GET_NEXT
must be adjusted in the Transformation Cockpit scenario. If the number range strategy is set to
“Increment” with ID = RENUMBER, the corresponding value is reserved on the productive client.
The global function uses the function module /SNP/PX0X_RFC_GET_NEXT_NUMBER, which is
called via RFC. The RFC should be provided as a connection from the MDT Staging client to the
MDT production client.
The source code of the adjusted global function GF_NUMBER_GET_NEXT is as follows:

11.2.13 Storing CO Keys in Another Client
As part of the MDT approach, certain situations require the processing of tables that necessitate
unique entries, specifically for CO keys. These CO keys must not only have a unique primary key
field but also combine all other fields to form a unique secondary index. When merging data from a
staging client into a production client, it is crucial to ensure that no conflicts arise in the production
client. Conflicts can cause errors when trying to create new unique keys. Correct handling ensures
the uniqueness of these keys. This function is necessary for critical tables that have an additional
unique index on non-primary key fields. The relevant keys include ONRAO, COKEY, and
COKEY2.

=====PAGE 979=====
979
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
Storing CO keys in a separate client helps to minimize the downtime on the target system during
the data migration. By reserving CO keys on the staging client from production clients, new data
that is created on the staging client can be seamlessly transferred to the production client. This
ensures that the CO keys remain consistent with the merged data and maintains data integrity.
11.2.13.1 Simplified representation of the standard CO process
1. Select the desired combination of return value and primary key from the following tables.
2. Optional: If no entry is available, create a new one.
3. Use the primary key of the entry as the target value for the global mapping.
The global mapping is used in other CO tables to establish a relation to characteristic com-
binations.
NOTE
After the forerunners ONRAO and COKEYS, it is necessary to copy the data from the
production client to the staging client. This synchronizes the tables between the staging
and production clients. To do so, use the function Refresh data in staging 1:1.
11.2.13.2 There are two cases to avoid when working with the shadow
client:
The user creates a table entry in the production system that has a different key but the same
characteristics.
The user creates a table entry in the production system that has the same key but a different
characteristic.
NOTE
The set of characteristic combinations required in the target is determined by the CO
forerunner and does not change after export.

=====PAGE 980=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
980
11.2.13.3 CO Keys and Import Parameters
11.2.13.3.1 COKEYS
Import parameter
IS_MERKMALE type COKEY_IS
NOTE
For unique field combinations, the unique CO key subnumber is returned. It is intended
to be used via RFC, but can also be used locally.
11.2.13.3.2 ONRAO

NOTE
For a unique combination, the index keys of the object number are created and the
object number is returned. It is intended to be used via RFC, but can also be used loc-
ally.

11.2.14 Coupling Number Ranges
MDT coupling is essential for the MDT procedure to run smoothly. It is mainly used in client merge
and multi-wave migration projects. The coupling of number ranges provides the following advant-
ages:
Efficiently updating client fields in SAP® S/4HANA
Minimizing downtime for operational organizational units
Supporting wave-based migrations with minimal disruptions
After a successful migration, you need a deletion transport for the MDT enhancement to restore the
production system in case of unexpected behavior.
The following chapters describe how to couple number ranges.
11.2.14.1 Coupling Number Ranges
NOTE
Number range coupling is only possible on request.
SAP systems include number range intervals that are used to retrieve consecutive number ranges.
You can use these number ranges in turn to retrieve unique identifiers for data that will later be
saved in the database. The intervals are client-dependent.
With the MDT approach, the data that you want to migrate to the production client is first imported
into the staging client. During the import, new identifiers must be assigned to the data – in many
cases directly from number range intervals. To ensure that the data can be moved successfully at a
later point in time, the identifiers must be unique in relation to the production client. This means that
the numbers used as identifiers must be reserved in the production client. This minimizes the risk
that the data to be migrated to the production clients contains collisions or duplicates.
Activating the coupling enables the usage of the function module extension NUMBER_GET_NEXT
for the selected coupled pair. If you activate the number range coupling between clients, every call
of the function module NUMBER_GET_NEXT leads to an increase in the interval level in the pro-
duction client, regardless on which client it was executed. The function module always returns the
number range received from the production client. The coupling was implemented in such a way

=====PAGE 987=====
987
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
that it does not impair the operation of the production client. Any problems that occur during coup-
ling must not block operations in the production system.
The coupling takes place in two specific clients (staging and production), which form a coupled pair.
You can perform the coupling for multiple coupled pairs. However, you can only use one client for
an active coupled pair. If you try to start a second coupled pair with an already used client, an error
appears during the activation. When staging is activated, the NRIV table entries in the staging client
are overwritten with the data from the production client. In addition, the interval status is decreased
by 10. The buffers for the number range with main memory buffering are also reset. This ensures
that numbers drawn from the staging client lead to an error. This in turn ensures that numbers are
always drawn from the production client. In addition, the interval level between the staging client
and production client is verified before the coupling is activated. The intervals that have a higher
level on the staging client are identified. These differences can later lead to issues in the staging cli-
ent. If the level was higher before the coupling started and was overwritten with a lower level, errors
can occur in the staging client. These errors occur because the retrieved number ranges are not
unique.
When activating the coupling, you can specify the number range to which the coupling is applied.
The scope is linked to the coupled pair. You can restrict the coupling to number ranges that are
required in the project or to number ranges that you do not want to synchronize between clients.
You can define additional number range exclusions for active coupled clients via transaction
/SNP/MDT_NREX. Once you have activated the coupling, it is no longer possible to add a number
range to the coupling scope. You can find the excluded number range in the table
/SNP/UP41NRIVRES.
NOTE
The newly created number ranges are automatically added to the active couplings. If
you do not want to synchronize these number ranges, you must exclude them manually
via transaction /SNP/MDT_NREX.
11.2.14.2 Activating the Number Range Coupling
Proceed as follows to activate the coupling of number ranges between clients.
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT_NRC.
The view Couple number ranges between clients opens.

=====PAGE 988=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation

NOTE

6. Click
Execute.
You have activated the coupling of number ranges between the clients.
NOTE

the system checks whether intervals exist with a higher level on the staging client.
If such intervals are identified, the system displays them for you so that you can
confirm their further activation. You can also stop this activation.

11.2.14.7 Daemon for Monitoring Number Ranges
This daemon identifies changes in number range intervals of the staging clients during the coupling
process. The level of the number range intervals in the staging client must not change. The daemon
compares the current levels of the number range intervals of the staging client with those levels
recorded in the table /SNP/UP41NRIVHLD during the coupling process. In doing so, the daemon
checks the values for discrepancies.
If the daemon determines that the current number range level in the staging client is higher than the
recorded level, it indicates that the number range interval has been increased. This should not be
the case during an ongoing coupling process.
All differences are recorded in the table /SNP/UP41MONHLD. This log contains the last difference
found for the interval so that unexpected changes in number range intervals can be checked.
The main purpose of this daemon is to ensure that no changes are made to the number ranges on
the staging client during the coupling process. In doing so, the daemon helps to maintain the integ-
rity of the coupling process.
You can only start the daemon during the coupling process. You can only execute one daemon for
a specific pair of linked clients. However, you can execute multiple daemons simultaneously for dif-

=====PAGE 992=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
992
ferent pairs. The daemon automatically stops if you terminate the coupling process via transaction
/SNP/MDT_NRDC.
11.2.14.7.1 Starting the Daemon for Monitoring Number Ranges
Proceed as follows to start the daemon:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT_DMON.
The application SNP MDT coupling daemon opens.
2. Select the staging client for the active coupling.
3. Select one of the two options:
As continuous check: The daemon works as a single background job and performs
number range checks continuously.
As periodic job: Successive number range checks are performed as separate back-
ground jobs.
4. Optional: Select a value for Wait time between checks (sec.). The daemon waits the spe-
cified time before performing the next number range check.
5. Select the Delete existing logs option to delete entries from the table
/SNP/UP41DMONLOG for staging and production clients.
6. Click
Execute.
You have started the daemon for monitoring number ranges.
11.2.14.7.2 Stopping the Daemon for Monitoring Number Ranges
The daemon automatically stops if you terminate the coupling process via transaction /SNP/MDT_
NRDC.
There are other ways to stop the daemon without terminating the coupling process:
In the customizing table /SNP/UP41DMONCFC, delete the parameter ACTIVE for at least
one coupling client. The daemon is stopped during the next iteration of the checks.
Stop the background job for the daemon via transaction SM37. The job has the prefix SNP_
MDT_DAEMON.

11.2.17 Limitations
This chapter explains the restrictions you need to take into account when using Minimized Down-
time on Target (MDT).
11.2.17.1 Verification and Data Quality
One of the primary challenges when using MDT is ensuring data accuracy and quality after all work
processes are completed on the production system (and on the staging client too). Verification
involves extensive checks to confirm that the data has been correctly transformed and loaded. Inac-
curacies can lead to significant issues post-migration. Ensuring that the data is consistent, accurate
and complete requires robust validation processes, which can be complex and time-consuming.
NOTE
Not all inconsistencies can be found using SNP Validate or Data Consistency Veri-
fication.
11.2.17.2 The Complexity of Mergers
Merging multiple entities (e.g. company codes) is a complex process. Each entity might have dis-
tinct data structures, business processes and rules. Harmonizing these differences into a unified
structure requires meticulous planning and execution. The complexity increases with the number of
companies involved and the extent of their differences. This makes the process more prone to
errors, which means that a successful implementation requires extensive expertise.
Minimized Downtime on Target can be combined with several complexity drivers such as:
Using Rule-Based Near Zero Downtime (RBNZD) to reduce the downtimes of organizational
units in the scope of the migration.
Splitting company codes on the source system or merging them on the target system.
Working with more than one staging clients for parallel testing.

=====PAGE 1000=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
1000
Reducing the cutover downtime on the target system further towards zero by sacrificing fall-
back scenarios and using clear validation and sign-off procedures.
NOTE
Such combinations require careful elaboration, estimation and planning.
11.2.17.3 Updating Data on Target Systems
Updating data in the target systems post-migration can be challenging. Data structures and busi-
ness requirements are likely to change after the initial transformation. Therefore, updating the tar-
get system to reflect these changes requires careful planning. The risk of disrupting ongoing
business operations while updating the data is a significant concern.
NOTE
When using MDT, updating the data on the production system is not allowed.
11.2.17.4 Deleting Data on Target Systems
The general procedure does not allow for data to be deleted or overwritten on the target system.
In MDT, the target production client is always the leading client, and data from the import is only
inserted (in the form of an INSERT ACCEPTING DUPLICATE KEYS). The MDT procedure does
not involve a DELETE or UPDATE (or MODIFY). While it is possible to alter data on the production
system in exceptional special cases, such cases must be carefully defined and implemented.
11.2.17.5 Postings in the Staging Area
Postings in the staging area, where data is temporarily stored during the transformation process,
can complicate the Staging procedure. Managing these postings to ensure that data flows correctly
from the staging area to the final target system is crucial. Any issues in the staging area can lead to
data inconsistencies or loss, impacting the overall success of the migration.
11.2.17.6 Space Consumption
MDT processes involving large volumes of data can consume significant storage space. This is par-
ticularly true for staging areas and backup environments. This is mainly due the framework of MDT.
As part of the process, additional client copies are created (e.g. staging client, paper bin client and

=====PAGE 1001=====
1001
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
load log client). During the migration processes, it is possible for large numbers of records to be
stored in these clients. Based on the size and scope of the project, this can have a large impact on
the system storage. Therefore, it must be ensured that more than enough storage is available on
the system. Efficiently managing space to avoid excessive storage costs while ensuring that per-
formance is not compromised is a key challenge.
11.2.17.7 Technical Runtimes
The technical runtime of MDT to merge data from staging to production clients depends greatly on
the specific project requirements, the size and complexity of the data being migrated, and the sys-
tem environment. However, experience has shown that the runtime of MDT is comparable to the
pure technical import runtime of the Transformation Cockpit (i.e. without mappings and trans-
formation rules, which typically make up most of the import runtime). Therefore, the runtime for
MDT is significantly shorter.
For other activities related to the migration of data to the staging client, other factors must be taken
into account:
11.2.17.7.1 SNP functions with longer runtimes
Transformation Cockpit: Contains mapping rules and transformation rules.
MDT Coupling for Number Get Next: Ensures continuous and gap-free number ranges.
Because this function utilizes RFC connections, it can slightly increase the runtime for large
sets of data.
NOTE
These two SNP functions are crucial for managing the efficiency and accuracy of the
data transformation process.
11.2.17.7.2 Other operations that significantly impact technical runtimes
S/4HANA conversions
Extensive checks on the staging client
Manual activities during the migration
Activities on request, e.g. a document split

=====PAGE 1002=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
1002
11.2.17.8 Fallback Scenarios During Go-Lives
During go-lives, it is possible for the MDT merge from the staging area into the production system
to fail or encounter issues. This results in gaps in the number ranges due to the number range coup-
lings. This can cause issues for certain non-buffered number ranges or number ranges that are not
allowed to have gaps.
11.2.17.9 General Information
Minimized Downtime on Target offers substantial benefits in terms of data consolidation and quality
improvement, but it also presents several significant challenges. To ensure a successful trans-
formation, organizations must be prepared to address issues related to data verification, complexity
of mergers, updates, deletions, postings in staging, space consumption, technical runtimes, fall-
back scenarios and number range management. Adequate planning, robust tools and expertise are
essential to mitigate these limitations and achieve the desired outcomes.
11.2.18 Delta Triggers and Delta Transfers
This chapter explains how to manage and synchronize changes in master data between staging
and production environments. This function ensures that changes made during the import step are
accurately reflected in the production environment. This ensures that data integrity is maintained
and allows for manual verification.
The process works as follows: First, MDT triggers are created. Next, the logged changes are trans-
ferred to the production client.
11.2.18.1 Creating MDT Triggers
Proceed as follows to create a MDT trigger:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT_TRIGGERS.
The program SNP delta triggers in the MDT staging client opens.
2. Select the desired tables.
3. Select the staging clients.
4. Select the option Create MDT triggers.

=====PAGE 1003=====
1003
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
5. Select which database operations you want to log in the previously selected tables.
6. Click
Execute.
You have created a MDT trigger.
NOTE
You can also delete the MDT trigger. To do so, select the option Delete MDT triggers in
step 4.
11.2.18.2 Delta Transfers
After creating the MDT trigger, you can perform a delta transfer to transfer the desired data to the
production area. This takes place on the production client.
Proceed as follows to perform a delta transfer:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/MDT_DELTA_TRANS.
The program SNP delta transfer opens.
2. Select the desired tables.
3. Select the production client. The staging client is selected automatically.
4. Define a target area ID.
NOTE
If multiple delta transfers are required, we recommend using different target area IDs.
5. Click
Execute.
The delta transfer has been performed.
NOTE
You can also reverse the delta transfer. To do so, start transaction /N/SNP/SG and use

11.3 RBNZD Approach
11.3.1 About RBNZD
The RBNZD RBNZD approach differs from a table-based NZD approach in terms of the application
of the rule base, such as selections, mappings or domain rules, etc., during each migration. In gene-
ral, near-zero downtime means that the productive source system(s) continue to be available
during the actual migration of the majority of the data. These source systems are only taken offline
to migrate the remaining data that was changed during the earlier migration(s). The downtime for
the last migration is mandatory, because there must be a cut at some point where users can no lon-
ger produce changes in order to ensure that all the data is migrated consistently to the target sys-
tem. As a result, the source systems where the changes occur can be kept running for most of the
migration and only have to be taken down during the final migration. The target system cannot be
kept online without separate effort.
The most important point for NZD to work is that the amount of data which is migrated becomes
smaller with each migration. The first migration, known as the initial load, is full scope and migrates
all the data while respecting the rule base. All subsequent migrations are called delta loads and are
restricted to the changes that occur at the database level, also while respecting the rule base. The-
refore, the changes form the basis for each delta load. Assuming a system with an almost constant
rate of changes, the delta loads get sequentially shorter because the logging periods shrink. The
changes that occur in the source systems are logged at the database level with triggers and stored
in separate tables.
11.3.1.1 Concept
11.3.1.1.1 Migration Object-based Approach
With the RBNZD approach, all data is migrated as part of the respective migration objects (e.g.
DEBI). The data is read and written directly from and to tables, but the functional composition of the
data in multiple tables is always taken into account. This ensures that with every migration of the
object, all of the corresponding rule base is utilized and that the object instances are transferred
consistently. Changes in an object instance lead to the complete deletion of the instance on the tar-
get system, and a complete re-migration from the source system is required. This might mean that,
due to a single table change, multiple tables have data deleted in a delta deletion run and inserted

=====PAGE 1005=====
1005
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
later on in a delta load (Delete/Insert Principle). This approach also covers cases where records fall
out of scope of the migration, for example due to priority switches or selection criteria. In special
cases, object instances are not deleted, but reset to the state they were in before the initial load
(Reset/Import Principle).
11.3.1.1.2 Rule Base Analysis
The analysis of the rule base is a crucial step in setting up the RBNZD scenario. Because RBNZD
is basically engine-independent, the rule base analysis converts relevant data from the given
engine into the RBNZD data model. Currently, only the Transformation Cockpit Transformation
Cockpit is fully supported as a migration engine. Note that only the engine migrates data, not
RBNZD itself.
The rule base analysis includes loading migration objects and tables from the engine, creating NZD
objects for all root tables, and creating relations between NZD objects and tables. Furthermore, the
analysis requires the scoping of tables to define whether a table is tracked and/or migrated. A table
that is in scope for tracking will result in the generation of a trigger, trigger table, collector table and
collector program. The migration scope determines whether the table extension is generated and
the delta deletion is executed.
11.3.1.1.3 Tracking Changes
The changes that occur in the source systems are logged at the database level with triggers and
stored in separate tables. Because RBNZD uses a migration object-based approach, it is man-
datory to resolve table changes to changes at the object instance level. This task is performed by
the collector. The rule base analysis (e.g. of a TC scenario) provides table connections that are
used to trace table changes back to corresponding object instances.
For each table in any RBNZD-enabled object, a trigger for all database operations (INSERT,
UPDATE and DELETE) is generated. The triggers identify every changed record and write the cor-
responding primary keys with the latest change timestamp to a separate trigger that is generated
for each tracked table. Because the triggers log each change at the database level, this method is
independent from the application that produces the data change. Because RBNZD is based on
migrating object instances, the collector goes through all triggered changes for a given time frame
and determines all relevant object keys that are affected by the changes, based on the table
connections that are derived from the rule base analysis. Technically, the collector crawls the table
chain from the original tables up to their corresponding root table. All determined root table keys

=====PAGE 1006=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
1006
are written to the corresponding collector table, which is generated based on the root table. The col-
lector tables build the basis for a delta load by being available as selection tables in the used migra-
tion engine. The triggers must be enabled before the initial load to ensure that all data changes
during the initial load are tracked.
11.3.1.1.3.1 Migrating Changes – Export
All migrations after the initial load are called delta loads. Here, the same migration objects are
migrated with the identical rule base as in the initial load. Only the collector tables are added as
additional selections for every NZD-compliant migration object. This reduces the migration scope to
only those object instances that have changed in the chosen time frame. The actual migration of
the object is performed by the engine in full fashion with all tables and with the whole rule base
being applied. A table-based migration is not possible using RBNZD.
11.3.1.1.3.2 Migrating Changes – Import and Deletion
The actual import is performed just like in a usual migration. The engine can use any import mode
to import the data.
Because the same records might be migrated in several loads, already migrated records must be
deleted in the target system first before they can be migrated again. Therefore, an import protocol
is written during the import, which contains every migrated record together with its corresponding
object key from the source system. This enables the delta deletion to identify all migrated records
via collected changes from the source system and is robust enough to handle all kinds of mappings
– even those that change the primary key – as well as object instances that fall out of the selection
scope. The deletion is performed by the RBNZD engine. Furthermore, when using MODIFY,
UPDATE or DELETE to migrate, not only the primary key and the object key are written to the pro-
tocol table, but also a version of the current record in the target system is persisted. If the cor-
responding object key is migrated in a subsequent load again, the old version of the record must be
restored instead of deleting the record.

11.3.4.3.1 Analyzing the Rule Base
This step transfers the data model of the engine into the RBNZD data model. Migration objects and
tables are created from Transformation Cockpit objects and tables. In addition, an NZD object is
created from each root table. Multiple root tables can also lead to one NZD object if they represent
the same table. An NZD object contains the key fields of the corresponding table. You can adjust
the key fields as required. Based on the NZD objects, the collector tables are subsequently gene-
rated and the table extension executed. Furthermore, the root tables are linked to the NZD objects
and the relations created between parent and child tables. The execution is parallelized using
batch processes on the control system.
Go to Preparation > Analysis of the rule base to refresh the analysis for certain objects if it beco-
mes necessary due to changes in the Transformation Cockpit data model. In the Preparation area,
you can start a complete analysis.
The tracking scope and migration scope are maintained automatically. However, you can also
change and extend these scopes manually in the Analysis of the rule base area in the Tables tab.
To do so, select all rows and click
Suggest scope to initially include all active tables whose
migration object is active and NZD-compliant in the tracking scope and migration scope. In the
Tracking scope and Migration scope columns, you can decide which entities you want to include
in the scopes. Furthermore, for table names, you can maintain patterns that impact the automatic
scoping.

11.3.4.3.9 Table Extension
The table extension allows you to assign a target key to the corresponding source key of the object
instance. Both the source key and target key are written to the corresponding protocol table during

=====PAGE 1022=====
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
1022
the import so that, if subsequently erased, it is possible to determine the target key for the changed
object keys. Therefore, the table extension takes the migration scope into account during exe-
cution.
The generation of the table extension runs in parallel for each migration object on the control sys-
tem. The key fields of a root table are generated as Transformation Cockpittable extensions to the
root table itself and to all its child tables. If an n:1 relationship arises from this, the key fields are
truncated until no n:1 relationship exists anymore or until no more key fields exist for the table
extension. If no more key fields exist, you must either change the structure of the migration object
or flag it as non-NZD-compliant.
If an n:1 relationship technically exists, but a de facto 1:1 relationship has been ensured, you can
define this via the NZD key fields area. In this area, specify the tables that you want the cardinality
check to ignore.

11.3.4.4 Collector
The collector is the software component that gathers the changes recorded by the trigger in the trig-
ger tables, returns them to object keys and compresses them. The existing rule base of the Trans-
formation Cockpit scenario is used as the basis for the table connections. The collector itself works
iteratively, i.e. it runs continuously at a certain interval on the source system. Such executions of
the collector are known as collector runs. A collector run is characterized by a unique ID (collector
ID). The only changes from the trigger table that are processed are changes that have not yet been
processed by a previous collector run. This process is determined by a field that is set during a col-
lector run and used for the corresponding data records in the trigger table.
When a collector starts processing, it schedules the next collector run as a job and uses the interval
specified in the configuration. Following this, all collector programs that were generated based on
the table scoping are executed with the number of processes specified in the configuration. Here,
one process processes all collector programs in one trigger table.
In the configuration menu, you can set the package size that is used to read from the trigger table.
The collector programs are then executed with the package from the trigger table. The object instan-
ces determined by the collector program are subsequently persisted in the collector table.
Once all collector programs for a package from the trigger table have been executed, the next
package is read. This continues until all data from the trigger table has been processed.

11.3.4.5 Delta Preparation
11.3.4.5.1 Generating the Delta SQL
NOTE
You only need to perform this step before the first delta load.
While generating the delta SQL, a free selection is generated for all root tables in the migration
scope. Using a subselect statement, the selection restricts the exports to the corresponding col-
lector tables for the collector run IDs in the global selection. Existing field selections are converted
and are therefore not lost. Existing free SQL is not changed, but only extended by the subselect.
Proceed as follows to generate a delta SQL:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/NZD.
2. Go to Delta preparation > Delta SQL.
3. Specify modules.
4. Specify objects.
5. Select the option Generate delta SQL.
6. Optional: Select the option Simulation if you only want to simulate the procedure at first.
7. Click
Execute.
The delta SQL has been generated.

11.3.4.5.3 Managing Delta Selections
Go to Delta preparation > Delta SQL > Delta selection to maintain delta selections. This step is
optional.
The delta selection enables a different definition for the assignment of the collector table and root
table. You can append zero, one or more root tables to another root table; the latter uses the chan-
ges of the other table(s) as the basis for the export. Note that one of the tables must be in the migra-
tion scope and have a table extension.
NOTE
As a rule, the “To” table is in the migration scope. This table is in the left-hand column
when entering the field connections in the Maintain field connection field. The “From”
table is in the right-hand column.
11.3.4.5.3.1 Field Connections
When you maintain field connections, the structure shows the key fields of the table that is in the
migration scope on the left-hand side. On the right-hand side, you can enter suitable fields from the
other table, which can be used for selection. All key fields of the table in the migration scope must
be linked to fields of the other table.
If both tables are in the migration scope, the table that was in the To table name column when crea-
ted is on the left-hand side when you maintain field connections.

=====PAGE 1031=====
1031
User Guide – CrystalBridge® Transformation
If only one table is in the migration scope, this table is on the left-hand side when you maintain field
connections.

3. Decide which collector IDs you want to use for the selection:
Collector IDs not executed: All collector run IDs that have not been migrated so far
All collector IDs: All collector run IDs are selected
Collector runs: One or more collector runs that you select manually
Names of delta transfers: All collector run IDs that have been used to perform a delta
transfer
Collector IDs from time: All collector runs as of the specified point in time
4. Optional: Select the option Simulation if you only want to simulate the procedure at first.
5. Click
Execute.

added.

migrated.
11.3.4.5.5 Setting the Run ID
The run ID is part of the table extension and relevant for the versioning of data records in order to
restore them in accordance with the reset/import principle. The initial value is 1. When you set the
run ID, you can restrict it to individual modules and objects.
You must increment the run ID before every delta load. We recommend incrementing it by 1, but
you can select any run ID.
Proceed as follows to set a run ID:
1. Start transaction /N/SNP/NZD.
2. Go to Delta preparation > Set run ID.
3. Specify modules.
4. Specify objects.
5. Specify any new run ID.
6. Optional: Select the option Simulation to initially only determine which modules, objects and
tables have been affected and whether the procedure can be performed successfully.
7. Click
Execute.
The run ID has been set for all tables below the selected modules and/or objects.
